approved: Communications Legislation Amendment (Deregulation and Other Measures) Bill 2015
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
This bill is part of a package that aims to cut red tape in broadcasting and telecommunications while keeping consumer protections.
It would simplify regulation by removing outdated requirements and giving regulators more discretion in fee collection and complaints handling.
The package would also allow the telecommunications industry to create a private scheme for managing phone numbers, subject to safeguards.
Streamline accounting and fee rules for commercial broadcasters by removing audit requirements and expanding who can declare earnings.
End duplicate reporting of media ownership changes to the ACMA.
Apply a single classification standard for all TV programs, including films.
Remove overlap in the ACMA's complaint and investigation processes.
Stop the ACCC from ordering carriers and service providers to submit tariff filings.
Repeal several outdated Acts that are no longer needed.
Commercial broadcasters, datacasting licensees, television broadcasters, carriers, carriage service providers, the ACMA, and the ACCC.

The amendment proposed is not related to the matters dealt with by the Communications Legislation Amendment (Deregulation and Other Measures) Bill 2015. That bill, as introduced, does not seek to amend the NBN Companies Act. The government moved the Communications Legislation Amendment (Deregulation and Other Measures) Bill to remove outdated regulation, claiming it has already cut over 3,000 pages of red tape and saved $300 million annually. Key measures include streamlining licence fee administration, removing duplicate control notifications, implementing a single TV classification scheme, repealing tariff-filing arrangements, reforming information collection powers, and enabling industry self-management of telephone numbering.

The Telecommunications (Numbering Charges) Amendment Bill 2015 makes consequential amendments to allow the telecommunications industry to self-manage telephone numbering resources, while ensuring the Australian Communications and Media Authority continues to collect $60 million in annual charges from carriage service providers.

The speaker argued the deregulation bills are a routine clean-up exercise that save nothing, despite previous bills saving $35 million and $350,000 respectively, and the opposition will not oppose them. The bills amend the Broadcasting Services Act and provide a framework for an industry-managed telephone numbering scheme, with support from the Communications Alliance, ACCAN, and Free TV Australia.

The speaker argued that the Communications Legislation Amendment (Deregulation and Other Measures) Bill 2015 is not a rudimentary cleanup, but includes significant deregulation, such as removing duplicate notification requirements and enabling the telecommunications industry to develop its own numbering scheme, potentially improving efficiency.

The speaker moved to disagree with a Senate amendment requiring nbn co to publish financial and deployment forecasts for 2015–2022, arguing the amendment is unrelated to the bill's purpose of streamlining regulation and reducing compliance burdens.
